# The suite's rules, in full

SUITE-RULES.md is the one-page list: each rule, its tier, and why in a sentence. This is every rule
in full: what it checks, exactly, why, how to fix a failure, and a wrong and a right example. It is
written for whoever fixes a failure, person or AI.

A **story** is a test carrying `@Story` or extending `StoryTest`. The story rules hold for stories
only; a test of your own that is not one is held to the hard rules (it checks something, and the
generated files around it stay as generated).

Run just the rules: `mvn test -Dgroups=rules` (in playwright-playground-com-tests).

## SR-01 · A story is in cases/

**What it checks.** Every story (a class extending StoryTest or carrying @Story) is in the cases/ folder (its package ends in .cases). A test of your own that is not a story may live anywhere under src/test/java.

**Why.** One folder holds every story, generated tests beside them. A person looking for what the suite checks finds it there, and can delete a stale story without touching the machinery the tests stand on (BaseTest, StoryTest, Story, the rules), which is one folder up.

**How to fix it.** Move the class into cases/ and change its package line to &lt;base>.cases. Import what it uses from one level up (BaseTest, StoryTest, Story).

Breaks the rule:

```java
// src/test/java/com/example/tests/stories/Engi101.java
package com.example.tests.stories;
```

Follows it:

```java
// src/test/java/com/example/tests/cases/Engi101.java
package com.example.tests.cases;

import com.example.tests.Story;
import com.example.tests.StoryTest;
```

## SR-02 · A story stands on StoryTest

**What it checks.** A story (a class carrying @Story) extends StoryTest, directly or through another class. A test of your own that is not a story is not held to it; extending BaseTest gives it the browser and the evidence.

**Why.** StoryTest is BaseTest (a test's browser, its numbered plain-English step log, the evidence of a failure: screenshot, the page's HTML, a trace) with the story's id in the log. A story that stands on neither runs blind and fails without a word of why.

**How to fix it.** Write "extends StoryTest" for a story; "extends BaseTest" for any other test that needs a browser.

Breaks the rule:

```java
class Engi101 {
```

Follows it:

```java
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {
```

## SR-03 · A story names its story

**What it checks.** A story class carries @Story with the story's id: @Story(value = "engi-101", title = "...").

**Why.** The id ties the test to the story in the team's tracker and in stories/done/: the run log prints it, a failure points back to it, and SR-17 and SR-18 check the two stay together.

**How to fix it.** Put @Story(value = "&lt;id>", title = "&lt;the story's title>") above the class, the id exactly as the story writes it.

Breaks the rule:

```java
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {
```

Follows it:

```java
@Story(value = "engi-101", title = "Learn More on the home page leads to Careers")
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {
```

## SR-04 · A story class is named after its id

**What it checks.** The class name is the @Story id with its letters and digits kept and the first made upper case, capitals aside: engi-101 is Engi101, INJ-592 is INJ592 (and Inj592 passes too). An id that starts with a digit gets "Story" in front. A requirement, the story's n-th acceptance criterion (engi-101-3), is the story's class name and _n: Engi101_3 (G-188).

**Why.** Anyone holding a story id finds its test by name, in cases/, without searching: that is what makes a stale story easy to delete. The file is named after the class, as Java requires.

**How to fix it.** Rename the class (and its file) to the name the message gives.

Breaks the rule:

```java
@Story(value = "engi-101", title = "...")
class LearnMoreTest extends StoryTest {
```

Follows it:

```java
@Story(value = "engi-101", title = "...")
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {
```

## SR-05 · Each story id is used once

**What it checks.** No two story classes carry the same @Story id (capitals aside); each requirement of a story (engi-101-1, engi-101-2) is its own id.

**Why.** One story, or one requirement of it, one test: a second class with the same id is a copy that drifts from the first, and deleting "the" test of a stale story leaves the other behind.

**How to fix it.** Keep one class per id. If the two check different things, they are two stories: give the second its own id and story file.

## SR-06 · A story is one test

**What it checks.** A story class has exactly one test method, of any kind JUnit runs (@Test, @TestFactory, @ParameterizedTest, @RepeatedTest, @TestTemplate): a parameterized test is one test run many times, each run its own outcome.

**Why.** A story is one visitor's journey with one outcome. Two tests in one story class are two outcomes, and the story that asked for both was two stories: splitting them keeps each failure pointing at one thing.

**How to fix it.** Keep the one test for the story's outcome. Anything else it checked is another story: write it up (stories/new/) and let it get its own class.

Breaks the rule:

```java
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {
    @Test void learnMore() { ... }
    @Test void applyNow() { ... }
}
```

Follows it:

```java
@Story(value = "engi-101", title = "Learn More on the home page leads to Careers")
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {

    @Test
    @DisplayName("Learn More on the home page leads to Careers")
    void story() {
        new HomePage(page).open()
                .click().learnMore()
                .verify().isLoaded();
    }
}
```

## SR-07 · A story has one check

**What it checks.** A story class calls .verify() exactly once.

**Why.** "One verify per story" (Ghost, 2026-09-28): a story states one outcome, and its test proves that one. A story with two checks was badly written and gets pushed back (stories/AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md). Arriving on a page needs no check of its own: every page checks it has loaded when a step lands on it.

**How to fix it.** No verify(): end the chain with the check the story's outcome asks for. Two or more: the story has two outcomes; push back and split it into stories.

Breaks the rule:

```java
.click().learnMore()
.verify().headingMentions("Careers")
...
.verify().showsTheJobSection();
```

Follows it:

```java
.click().learnMore()
.verify().isLoaded();
```

## SR-08 · The check comes last

**What it checks.** After a story's .verify(), nothing else is done: no click(), enter(), check(), uncheck(), clear(), read(), execute(), navigateTo() or open().

**Why.** The check is the story's outcome, so the story ends there. A step after it is either a second outcome in disguise, or a step the check did not cover.

**How to fix it.** Move the steps before the verify(), or if they lead to a second outcome, make that a story of its own.

Breaks the rule:

```java
.verify().isLoaded()
.click().applyNow();
```

Follows it:

```java
.click().applyNow()
.verify().showsTheJobSection();
```

## SR-09 · A story's test reads as its title

**What it checks.** The story's @Test carries @DisplayName("...").

**Why.** The report and the run log show the display name: with the story's title there, a person who never opens the code reads which story passed or failed.

**How to fix it.** Put @DisplayName("&lt;the story's title>") on the test.

## SR-10 · A story uses page objects, not Playwright

**What it checks.** A story class does not import com.microsoft.playwright, call .locator( or .getBy..., or call the page itself (page.): it goes through page objects.

**Why.** A story reads like the story because every step is a page method named for what a visitor does ("click().learnMore()"). Locators and browser calls in a test hide what it does, break when the site changes in many places at once, and skip the step log and the waits the page objects give.

**How to fix it.** Add the element to the page's Elements enum (ai/recipes/add-an-element.md) and an action or check that uses it (add-an-action.md); call that from the story.

Breaks the rule:

```java
page.locator("xpath=//a[@aria-label='Learn More']").click();
```

Follows it:

```java
new HomePage(page).open()
        .click().learnMore()
```

## SR-11 · A story does not assert

**What it checks.** A story class uses no assertions: no assert, assertTrue/assertEquals/assertFalse/assertThat, Assertions., fail(.

**Why.** Checks live in the pages' verify() methods, built on Checks, which log the step and fail in plain English ("Expected the email input to hold ..."). An assertion in a story fails with "expected true", logs nothing, and is a second check SR-07 cannot see.

**How to fix it.** Add the check to the page's VerifyActions (ai/recipes/add-an-action.md) and end the chain with verify().&lt;that check>.

Breaks the rule:

```java
assertTrue(page.url().endsWith("/careers"));
```

Follows it:

```java
.verify().isLoaded();
```

## SR-12 · Nothing sleeps

**What it checks.** No Thread.sleep( or waitForTimeout( (a sleep by another name) anywhere in the tests and pages (core/ aside), and no shortenWaits( outside the suite's own harness.

**Why.** A sleep is too long on a fast day and too short on a slow one: the test gets slower and still flaky. WaitActions waits for the thing itself (an element to show or go away, a URL), exactly as long as needed.

**How to fix it.** Wait for what the step needs with WaitActions (ai/recipes/wait-for-a-slow-page.md).

Breaks the rule:

```java
Thread.sleep(2000);
```

Follows it:

```java
WaitActions.waitForInvisibilityOf(page, HomeElements.LOADING_SPINNER);
```

## SR-13 · No regular expressions in tests and pages

**What it checks.** No java.util.regex, Pattern.compile, .matches(, .replaceAll(, .replaceFirst( or .split( in the tests and pages (core/ aside): each of the last four takes a regular expression.

**Why.** Tests and pages are read and changed by people who aren't programmers; a regular expression is where they stop understanding. Plain strings say what they mean.

**How to fix it.** Compare plain strings (Checks.hasText, containsText; WaitActions.sameText). If a pattern is truly needed, put it in a helper in core/ with a plain name, and call that.

## SR-14 · A test switched off says why

**What it checks.** Every @Disabled says why, in its reason: @Disabled("the site's search is down, KNOWN-ISSUES.md #3"). A bare @Disabled, or one with an empty reason, is a warning; so is anything in pom.xml that switches tests off or ignores their failures: skipTests, maven.test.skip, testFailureIgnore, skipAfterFailureCount, an &lt;excludes> list.

**Why.** A test switched off without a word hides a failure and is forgotten; with its reason, the next person knows whether it can come back. Switching tests off in the pom (its YOURS blocks allow properties) would silence the whole suite, these rules included, while mvn test still says BUILD SUCCESS.

**How to fix it.** Give the @Disabled its reason, or delete the test (a stale story: its class in cases/ and its file in stories/done/), or fix it. Take the setting out of pom.xml; to run fewer tests for a while, say so on the command line (-Dgroups=smoke, -Dtest=...), where it lasts one run.

Breaks the rule:

```java
@Disabled
@Test
void searchFindsResults() {
```

Follows it:

```java
@Disabled("search is down on the site since 2026-10-01: KNOWN-ISSUES.md")
@Test
void searchFindsResults() {
```

## SR-15 · YOURS blocks keep both marker lines

**What it checks.** Every file has as many YOURS opening lines as closing ones, counting only marker lines that are comments (starting with //, &lt;!-- or #): exactly the lines regenerating reads as markers.

**Why.** Regenerating keeps what is between a block's two marker lines, and only that. With a marker gone, whatever was in the block is lost the next time the suite is regenerated.

**How to fix it.** Put the missing line back exactly as it was: // ==== YOURS (name): ... ==== and // ==== END YOURS (name) ====.

## SR-16 · Generated files change only inside YOURS blocks

**What it checks.** Every file Suite Builder generated (listed with a fingerprint in src/test/resources/suite-rules/fingerprints.txt) is still there, and its text outside the YOURS blocks is exactly as generated. That includes the rules themselves: SuiteRules.java, SuiteRulesTest.java and SUITE-RULES.md. A change to the suite's guidance text (a generated Markdown file that is not a rule: the stories' and recipes' instructions, the glossary, the READMEs) is reported as a warning, not a failure (G-184).

**Why.** Regenerating the suite (a new crawl of a changed site) rewrites everything outside YOURS blocks, so a change made there silently disappears. And the rules are only worth something if nobody, person or AI, can quietly edit or delete them to make a failing test pass.

**How to fix it.** Move your change into a YOURS block or a file of your own, and put the rest back: regenerating restores it (suite build &lt;project>, which keeps everything in YOURS blocks). To change a rule, change Suite Builder, not the generated suite. A warning on guidance text needs nothing now; a change worth keeping goes into Suite Builder too, or the next regeneration rewrites it.

## SR-17 · Every story in stories/done/ has its test

**What it checks.** For each story file in stories/done/ (README.md aside), a story class carries its id in @Story, or one of its requirements does (engi-101-1). The id is the first word shaped like INJ-592 in the file name, else in the story's text above any ---- line, else the file name.

**Why.** stories/done/ is the record of which stories the suite checks. A story there without a test claims coverage that isn't there.

**How to fix it.** Implement the story (stories/AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md), or move it back to stories/new/, or, if it is stale, delete it.

## SR-18 · Every story test has its story in stories/done/

**What it checks.** For each story class, a story file in stories/done/ has its @Story id, or, for a requirement (engi-101-3), its story's id.

**Why.** The story file is the test's reason to exist, in the words of whoever asked for it; without it nobody can tell whether the test still checks something wanted. Together with SR-17 it means a stale story is retired by deleting both, and forgetting one is caught.

**How to fix it.** Add the story to stories/done/ (its words, with the IMPLEMENTED note naming this class), or, if the story is stale, delete this class too.

## SR-19 · Every test checks something

**What it checks.** Every test method (@Test, @ParameterizedTest, @RepeatedTest; the generated tests' too) checks at least one thing: a .verify() chain, a Checks call, or an assertion, in the method itself or in a method of the same class it calls (helper() or this.helper()). Checks.assume is not a check: it skips a test whose data is not there. A story is held to exactly one .verify() by SR-07 instead.

**Why.** A test that only acts (opens a page, clicks a link) and checks nothing passes whenever nothing throws: it can't tell the right page from the wrong one, and a green run says less than it seems. Even the plainest test ends by saying what it expected, if only that the page it reached has loaded (Ghost, 2026-09-28).

**How to fix it.** End the test with the check it is for: .verify().isLoaded() on the page it reaches at the least, or a Checks call (Checks.isOnPath for a page with no page class).

Breaks the rule:

```java
new HomePage(page).open()
        .click().goToAbout();
```

Follows it:

```java
new HomePage(page).open()
        .click().goToAbout()
        .verify().isLoaded();
```

## SR-20 · Account files stay out of git

**What it checks.** .gitignore leaves out secrets/*.login, and git tracks no file in secrets/ but its README.md (core/Credentials, G-159).

**Why.** An account in git is an account everyone with the repository has, and every copy of it handed on; a suite travels to dev teams, pipelines and tracker apps. The account files are each person's own, written blank in every fresh copy.

**How to fix it.** Put secrets/*.login back in .gitignore; for a file already committed, git rm --cached it, then change that account's password.

## SR-21 · A done story's notes name every criterion, by its number

**What it checks.** For each story in stories/done/ with a list of acceptance criteria (the list under its line naming them, "Acceptance Criteria:", above any ---- note) and tested by requirement (&lt;id>-&lt;n>, G-188): every criterion number from 1 to the list's length is a story test's id or named in its notes (a Tests: line's &lt;id>-&lt;n>, or a Not implemented line starting with the number), and no test or note names a number past the list. A story tested as a whole (its bare id) is left alone.

**Why.** A criterion's number is its test's name (&lt;id>-&lt;n>): a list edited after its tests were written moves every number after the edit, so a test checks one criterion under another's number, and a criterion left out of the notes is a part of the story nobody checks, or says is unchecked (trial 7: 3 of 3 list edits renumbered tested stories).

**How to fix it.** Implement each criterion named as &lt;id>-&lt;n>, or add a Not implemented line for it to the story's IMPLEMENTED note (&lt;n> &lt;the criterion>: &lt;what is needed>). A list changed after its tests: put it back as it was; a dropped criterion stays in the list, answered "drop" under a Not implemented line.

## SR-22 · One element, one name

**What it checks.** In each Elements enum, two constants with the same locator (its first string, without the Playwright prefix and visibility filter a generated one carries), at least one of them in a YOURS block. Two generated ones are the crawl's, never a story's, and are left alone.

**Why.** Every test then reaches one element two ways, and a locator fixed under one name is still broken under the other; two stories written apart (two branches) each add their own name for the same button and merge without a conflict.

**How to fix it.** Keep one name, delete the other constant, and point every use of it at the one kept (search the tests and pages for its name). Before adding an element, search the Elements for its locator (ai/recipes/add-an-element.md).
